book.title: Computer Networking: Principles, Protocols and Practice

easy.prompt: What is the main purpose of layering in the Internet protocol stack?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each layer provides a service to the layer above while hiding lower-layer details

choices.label: B
choices.body: Each layer is a separate physical box that packets must visit in order

choices.label: C
choices.body: Layering exists so every router must parse HTTP headers

choices.label: D
choices.body: Layering means DNS runs below the physical signaling layer

easy.hint: Next step: ask what service each layer offers the one above it, not where boxes sit.
easy.explanation: Layering modularizes functions so each layer uses the service of the layer below. This lets Ethernet change without rewriting HTTP.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: An HTTP GET becomes a TCP segment with ports and sequence numbers. Step 2: IP wraps it with src/dst addresses and TTL. Step 3: Ethernet wraps that with MACs and FCS. Step 4: Each layer is processed peer-to-peer without exposing its internals upward.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: x
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Routers forward on IP headers; they do not need HTTP to route.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DNS is an application-layer service running above transport, not below physics.

easy.prompt: In the TCP/IP model, at which layer does IP provide host-to-host delivery?
easy.hint: Next step: place TCP/UDP first, then ask what sits directly beneath them.
easy.explanation: IP delivers datagrams host-to-host at the internet layer, below TCP/UDP and above link technologies.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: App bytes enter a socket and TCP adds ports plus sequence number 1000. Step 2: IP adds header 192.0.2.1->203.0.113.7, TTL=64, proto=TCP. Step 3: The link adds MACs and forwards the frame; IP stays intact end-to-end.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Applications use TCP/UDP sockets; IP is one layer below them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: TCP and UDP live at transport; IP sits beneath them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Ethernet/Wi-Fi frame IP packets; IP itself is the layer above the link.

easy.prompt: Encapsulation as data moves down the sender stack means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each layer wraps the payload from above with its own header (and sometimes trailer)

choices.label: B
choices.body: IP addresses are replaced by MAC addresses for the whole Internet

choices.label: C
choices.body: Headers are stripped off at the sender and never re-added

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only the application layer ever adds a header

easy.hint: Next step: trace one message down: segment inside datagram inside frame.
easy.explanation: Each layer adds its header around the higher-layer payload. A TCP segment becomes the payload of an IP datagram inside an Ethernet frame.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: TCP builds segment seq=5000, ack=0, SYN set. Step 2: IP encapsulates it: 10.0.0.5->93.184.216.34, len=60. Step 3: Ethernet encapsulates that: src aa:..:01 -> dst gw mac, EtherType 0x0800 plus FCS.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: IP addresses stay end-to-end; MACs are rewritten hop-by-hop on each link.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The sender adds headers going down; receivers and routers process them, not pre-strip them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Transport, network, and link layers all add their own headers/trailers.

easy.prompt: What does DNS primarily map?

choices.label: A
choices.body: TCP port numbers to process names on a host

choices.label: B
choices.body: URLs directly to HTML page contents

choices.label: D
choices.body: IP addresses to globally routable MAC addresses

easy.hint: Next step: separate naming (who) from addressing (where) from delivery (how).
easy.explanation: DNS resolves names like www.example.com to A/AAAA records holding addresses. Fetching the page itself is HTTP's job.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Stub sends A query for www.example.com. Step 2: Resolver returns 93.184.216.34 with TTL=300. Step 3: Only then does TCP SYN go to that address; DNS never carried the HTML.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Local port tables name services on a host; DNS is Internet-wide naming.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: HTTP fetches resources; DNS only supplies the address records.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: ARP/ND maps IP to link-layer addresses on one subnet; DNS maps names to IPs.

easy.prompt: Which statement best separates a hostname, an IP address, and a MAC address?

choices.label: A
choices.body: They are three names for the exact same identifier

choices.label: B
choices.body: Hostnames are burned into NIC hardware at the factory

choices.label: C
choices.body: Hostname names the host, IP address locates it on the internetwork, MAC identifies the NIC on one link

choices.label: D
choices.body: IP addresses name the owner and MAC addresses route globally

easy.hint: Next step: ask the scope of each: name scope, internetwork scope, single-link scope.
easy.explanation: Names are user-friendly, IPs are hierarchical locators for routing, and MACs are flat link identifiers. Each layer uses the right one.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: User types example.com (name). Step 2: DNS returns 93.184.216.34 (locator) used in the IP header end-to-end. Step 3: On each hop Ethernet uses local MACs, rewritten at every router.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: They live at different layers with different scopes and formats.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MACs are burned into NICs; hostnames are administrative DNS data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: IPs locate interfaces hierarchically; MACs are flat and only significant on one link.

easy.prompt: Packet switching shares a link among many flows mainly by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Requiring all senders to transmit simultaneously in lockstep

choices.label: B
choices.body: Reserving a fixed circuit for every host pair at all times

choices.label: C
choices.body: Giving each flow its own physical wire

choices.label: D
choices.body: Interleaving packets on demand so idle senders waste no reserved capacity

easy.hint: Next step: contrast reserved circuits with on-demand packet interleaving.
easy.explanation: Packet switching multiplexes statistically: packets from whoever has data go next. Idle users consume no capacity, unlike reserved circuits.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Host A sends pkt seq=1 (1500 B) then goes idle. Step 2: The link immediately carries host B's pkt instead of idling on A's reservation. Step 3: A queue holds bursts; no per-call setup was needed.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Senders transmit independently; the multiplexer interleaves arrivals.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is circuit switching, the opposite of packet sharing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sharing means one wire carries many flows interleaved, not one wire each.

easy.prompt: Transmission delay versus propagation delay differ in that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: They are synonyms for router queueing time

choices.label: B
choices.body: Transmission is time to push bits onto the link; propagation is time for a bit to travel the link

choices.label: C
choices.body: Transmission delay ignores packet size and link rate

choices.label: D
choices.body: Propagation delay is reduced by buying more bandwidth

easy.hint: Next step: write L/R for transmission and d/s for propagation, then compare.
easy.explanation: Transmission delay = packet length / link rate; propagation = distance / signal speed. One shrinks with faster links, the other with shorter distance.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: A 12,000-bit packet on a 10-Mbps link takes L/R = 1.2 ms to clock out. Step 2: Over 200 km of fiber at ~2e8 m/s it then propagates ~1.0 ms. Step 3: Trace shows serialization at the sender followed by flight time.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Queueing is waiting in buffers, distinct from both pushing bits and signal flight.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Transmission delay is exactly L/R, so size and rate define it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bandwidth changes L/R, not distance/speed which sets propagation.

easy.prompt: The end-to-end principle argues that reliable file transfer should be checked…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Entirely inside routers, which see every packet

choices.label: B
choices.body: By DNS resolvers during name lookup

choices.label: C
choices.body: By Ethernet FCS alone on each hop

choices.label: D
choices.body: By the endpoints, because only they know the complete file and its correctness

easy.hint: Next step: ask who ultimately knows the file is complete and correct.
easy.explanation: Link reliability does not guarantee end-to-end file correctness, so endpoints must verify. Network help is optional; endpoint checks are necessary.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Sender TCP sends bytes 0-9999 with seq numbers and checksums. Step 2: Each link's FCS catches wire errors hop-by-hop yet a router bug could still corrupt data. Step 3: Receiver reassembly plus app hash confirms the whole file.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Routers forward quickly and may still misdeliver; endpoints must verify.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DNS resolves names; it never sees file bytes to validate them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: FCS protects one hop; it cannot detect errors above the link or missing segments.

easy.prompt: A stub resolver differs from an authoritative nameserver in that the stub…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Stores the master copy of every domain on the Internet

choices.label: C
choices.body: Assigns MAC addresses on the LAN

choices.label: D
choices.body: Asks on behalf of the app while authoritative servers hold the zone's records

easy.hint: Next step: ask who holds zone data versus who asks recursively.
easy.explanation: Stubs query; recursive resolvers iterate; authoritative servers own the zone data. No single server holds everything.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: App stub sends RD=1 query for example.com to 8.8.8.8. Step 2: The recursive resolver walks root->TLD->authoritative with referrals. Step 3: The authoritative reply AA=1 returns A=93.184.216.34.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Authority is distributed per zone; resolvers cache copies, not masters of all zones.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: BGP runs between routers; DNS servers answer name queries on port 53.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DHCP/ND handle LAN addressing, not DNS authority.

easy.prompt: Which transport protocol is connection-oriented with reliable in-order byte delivery?
easy.hint: Next step: ask which protocol handshakes, acks, and retransmits.
easy.explanation: TCP sets up a connection, numbers bytes, acks receipt, and retransmits loss. UDP is connectionless best-effort.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Client sends SYN seq=0. Step 2: Server replies SYN-ACK seq=9000 ack=1. Step 3: Data bytes 1-1460 flow with cumulative ACKs and retransmit on loss.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ARP resolves IP to MAC on a LAN, not end-to-end transport.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ICMP carries control messages like ping, not app byte streams.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: UDP sends datagrams with no connection, ordering, or retransmission.

easy.prompt: UDP is usually preferred over TCP when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every byte must arrive in order without loss

choices.label: B
choices.body: A handshake must precede any data

choices.label: C
choices.body: Low latency matters more than guaranteed delivery, as in live media or DNS

choices.label: D
choices.body: A fast sender must be throttled by the receiver

easy.hint: Next step: ask whether the app tolerates loss or can retry itself.
easy.explanation: UDP exposes raw datagrams with no retransmission delay. Apps that handle loss or repeat queries avoid TCP's cost.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: DNS query ID=0x1111 goes out as one UDP datagram. Step 2: Reply returns in 1 RTT or the client retries. Step 3: No SYN handshake or retransmission buffers delayed the exchange.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That requirement favors TCP, not UDP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: UDP has no setup; TCP uses the 3-way handshake.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Window-based flow control is a TCP feature, not UDP.

easy.prompt: A socket identifying one endpoint of a TCP connection is…

choices.label: C
choices.body: An IP address plus a port number

easy.hint: Next step: combine the host locator with the process demultiplexer.
easy.explanation: Sockets bind (IP, port); a connection is the pair of sockets. Ports demultiplex among processes on a host.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Server listens on 0.0.0.0:80. Step 2: Client 10.0.0.5:52344 sends SYN to 93.184.216.34:80. Step 3: The four-tuple uniquely names the connection both ways.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: MACs name NICs on one link; sockets need IP plus port end-to-end.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Paths name resources; sockets name transport endpoints.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Names resolve to IPs but do not identify a port/process.

easy.prompt: Well-known port 80 versus 443 differ in that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Ports determine the IP address of the server

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both are reserved for DNS queries

choices.label: C
choices.body: Port 80 is default HTTP while 443 is default HTTPS over TLS

choices.label: D
choices.body: Port 80 is encrypted and 443 is cleartext

easy.hint: Next step: map the port to the service and security wrapper.
easy.explanation: Ports select the service; TLS on 443 wraps HTTP in encryption. The IP still selects the host.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: SYN to port 80 begins cleartext HTTP GET /. Step 2: SYN to port 443 begins TLS ClientHello before any HTTP. Step 3: Server demultiplexes by dst port to different handlers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: IPs select hosts; ports select processes on that host.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DNS uses port 53, not 80/443.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Reversed: 443 carries TLS-encrypted HTTP, 80 is cleartext.

easy.prompt: The first packet of a TCP three-way handshake carries…
easy.hint: Next step: recite the flag order: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
easy.explanation: Client SYN opens, server SYN-ACK accepts, client ACK confirms. Sequence numbers synchronize both directions.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Client sends SYN seq=0, ack=0. Step 2: Server sends SYN seq=7000 ack=1. Step 3: Client sends ACK ack=7001 and data may follow.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: RST aborts a connection rather than opening it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: FIN tears a connection down, it does not open one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A lone ACK completes the handshake; it never opens one.

easy.prompt: The purpose of random initial sequence numbers (ISN) is mainly to…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Protect against spoofed segments from prior connections

easy.hint: Next step: ask what an attacker could do with predictable seq numbers.
easy.explanation: Random ISNs stop blind injection of forged segments that guess the next sequence. They are not encryption.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Client picks ISN=0xA41F0000 and sends SYN. Step 2: Attacker guessing seq=0 fails; receiver rejects off-window data. Step 3: Only the true peer tracking ack=ISN+1 continues.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ISNs add security, not speed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ISNs are public headers; TLS encrypts payload.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ports are chosen separately from sequence numbers.

easy.prompt: TCP detects a lost segment primarily via…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Missing cumulative ACKs: duplicate ACKs or a retransmission timeout

easy.hint: Next step: follow the ACK stream and notice which seq never gets covered.
easy.explanation: Receivers ack the next expected byte; gaps trigger duplicate ACKs and timers. The sender then retransmits the hole.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Sender transmits seq 1000, 2000, 3000. Step 2: Segment 1000 lost; receiver sends dup ACKs for 1000 on later arrivals. Step 3: Sender fast-retransmits seq=1000 without waiting for timeout.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 404 is app-level not-found, not transport loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DNS failures never signal TCP segment loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Preambles synchronize a link; they do not ack byte streams.

easy.prompt: TCP flow control exists to…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Keep a fast sender from overrunning the receiver's buffers

easy.hint: Next step: distinguish receiver capacity (flow) from network capacity (congestion).
easy.explanation: The receiver advertises rwnd in ACKs; the sender limits unacked data to min(rwnd, cwnd).
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Receiver advertises rwnd=8000 in ACK ack=5000. Step 2: Sender with 20000 bytes ready sends only 8000. Step 3: As the app reads, rwnd=16000 opens and sending resumes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Routing picks paths; flow control paces one connection.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DNS resolves names; windows regulate senders.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is congestion control, not receiver flow control.

easy.prompt: Network congestion means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A switch learned too many MACs

choices.label: B
choices.body: A host lacks a default gateway

choices.label: D
choices.body: Demand exceeds what links and buffers can carry, so queues grow and drops occur

easy.hint: Next step: compare offered load with link capacity and watch the queue.
easy.explanation: Overload shows as delay and loss. Senders must slow down; fixing a gateway or cache does not help.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Two 10-Mbps flows enter a 10-Mbps link. Step 2: Queue trace grows 0->40 packets, RTT doubles. Step 3: Tail drop of seq=8000 triggers dup ACKs and window cut.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: MAC table limits affect LAN flooding, not bandwidth contention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Missing routes break reachability but are not overload.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Expiry causes a lookup, not link overload.

easy.prompt: An IP router's primary job is to…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Forward packets between networks using routing tables

choices.label: D
choices.body: Assign IP addresses to LAN hosts

easy.hint: Next step: match dst IP against prefixes and pick the next hop.
easy.explanation: Routers look up destination prefixes and send toward the next hop. DHCP, TLS, and DNS are different boxes' jobs.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Packet arrives dst=203.0.113.77. Step 2: Table has 203.0.113.0/24 via eth1, 0.0.0.0/0 via eth0. Step 3: Longest match sends it out eth1 with TTL-1.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Resolvers do name translation, not routers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: TLS termination is a proxy/app function, not routing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is DHCP on a LAN, not core IP forwarding.

easy.prompt: A host's default gateway is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The longest BGP prefix in the world

choices.label: B
choices.body: The on-subnet router used to reach off-subnet destinations

choices.label: C
choices.body: The DNS server that resolves all names

easy.hint: Next step: ask where non-local packets go first on the LAN.
easy.explanation: Hosts send off-subnet traffic to the gateway's LAN IP; the gateway forwards onward.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Host 10.0.0.5/24 pings 8.8.8.8 (non-local). Step 2: It ARPs for gateway 10.0.0.1's MAC and frames the packet there. Step 3: Gateway routes with TTL-1 toward the Internet.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: BGP tables live in routers; hosts need only a default.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DNS and default routing solve different problems.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Remote MACs are unknown; packets go to the gateway's MAC.

easy.prompt: How many bits in a standard IPv4 address?
easy.hint: Next step: count dotted-quad octets times 8.
easy.explanation: IPv4 uses 32-bit dotted quads. 128 bits is IPv6; 48 bits is Ethernet MAC.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Address 192.0.2.1 is 4 octets. Step 2: 4 x 8 = 32 bits on the wire. Step 3: Header shows version=4, src/dst 32 bits each.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 64 bits matches no standard IP version length.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 16 bits is a TCP/UDP port, not an IPv4 address.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 128 bits is an IPv6 address.

easy.prompt: A home NAT router lets…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Carry IPv6-only traffic with no translation

choices.label: B
choices.body: Many private hosts share one public IPv4 address via port translation

choices.label: C
choices.body: Mint unlimited new public IPs per host

easy.hint: Next step: track the (private IP, port) to (public IP, port) mapping.
easy.explanation: NAT rewrites outbound tuples and reverses replies. It conserves addresses but breaks direct inbound reachability.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: 192.168.1.5:5000 -> 93.184.216.34:80 becomes 198.51.100.1:60001 -> 93.184.216.34:80. Step 2: Reply reverses the mapping. Step 3: Unsolicited inbound to 198.51.100.1:60001 without a mapping drops.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Classic NAT is an IPv4 workaround; NAT64 is a separate mechanism.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: NAT conserves addresses; it creates no new public ones.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DNSSEC is about DNS authenticity, not address sharing.

easy.prompt: IPv6 addresses are how long, and why does it matter?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 128 bits, vastly expanding address space beyond IPv4

easy.hint: Next step: compare 2^32 with 2^128 and the need for NAT.
easy.explanation: 128-bit space restores end-to-end addressing. Hosts use SLAAC or DHCPv6 instead of NAT conservation.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: IPv4 header carries 32-bit src/dst. Step 2: IPv6 header carries 128-bit src 2001:db8::5 to dst. Step 3: The same link carries far more unique endpoints without translation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 16 bits is port length, not IP length.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 32 bits is IPv4; IPv6 quadruples the length.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 48 bits is Ethernet MAC length, not IPv6.

easy.prompt: ping uses which protocol to test reachability?

choices.label: C
choices.body: ICMP echo request and echo reply

easy.hint: Next step: look for type 8 out and type 0 back.
easy.explanation: ICMP echo probes a host; replies measure RTT. TCP/ARP/DNS do different jobs.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Host sends ICMP type=8 code=0 seq=1 to 8.8.8.8. Step 2: Target returns type=0 with same payload. Step 3: Sender computes RTT from timestamps.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Zone transfers copy DNS data; they do not probe liveness.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ping needs no ports or SYN; ICMP suffices.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: ARP stays on one LAN; it never crosses routers.

easy.prompt: An IPv4 subnet mask (or prefix length) is used to…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Split the address into network prefix and host parts

easy.hint: Next step: AND the address with the mask to find the subnet.
easy.explanation: Masking tells hosts what is local versus what needs the gateway. Encryption and ports are unrelated.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: 10.0.5.23/24 has prefix 10.0.5.0. Step 2: AND with 255.255.255.0 confirms host part .23. Step 3: Packet to 10.0.5.99 goes direct; to 8.8.8.8 goes via gateway.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: DNS resolves names, not masks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: IPsec/TLS encrypt; masks only partition addresses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Ports are transport endpoints on a host.

easy.prompt: Forwarding versus routing differ in that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Forwarding builds BGP policy and routing sends packets

choices.label: C
choices.body: Routing happens per packet and forwarding happens yearly

choices.label: D
choices.body: Forwarding moves each packet to the next hop; routing builds the tables forwarding uses

easy.hint: Next step: separate the per-packet data plane from the control plane.
easy.explanation: Forwarding is a fast table lookup per packet; routing protocols (OSPF/BGP) compute those tables over time.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: OSPF converges and installs 10.1.0.0/16 via eth2. Step 2: Each arriving packet dst=10.1.5.5 looks up eth2 in nanoseconds. Step 3: A link failure re-runs routing; forwarding entries update.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Reversed: routing builds tables, forwarding sends.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One sends packets, the other computes paths — different planes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reversed: forwarding is per packet, routing is background.

easy.prompt: Which IPv4 block is private (RFC 1918) and not routed publicly?
easy.hint: Next step: recall the three private ranges versus loopback and multicast.
easy.explanation: Private addresses are reusable per LAN and need NAT to reach the Internet. The others are public, loopback, or multicast.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Host 10.0.0.5 sends to 93.184.216.34. Step 2: NAT rewrites src to public 198.51.100.1. Step 3: Replies return to the public address, never to 10.x directly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is public anycast DNS space, not private.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is multicast, not private unicast.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is loopback on the local host.

easy.prompt: Framing at the link layer provides…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Delimiters, addresses, and error checks wrapping each network datagram

easy.hint: Next step: list what a frame adds around the IP packet.
easy.explanation: Frames mark start/end, carry link addresses, and add FCS so receivers detect wire errors per hop.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: IP datagram 10.0.0.5->10.0.0.9 enters Ethernet. Step 2: Frame adds dst/src MACs, EtherType 0x0800, payload, FCS. Step 3: Receiver checks FCS before passing the datagram up.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Routing is network-layer; framing is single-hop.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Cache-Control is HTTP, not link framing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DNS resolves names at the app layer.

easy.prompt: MAC addresses are…

choices.label: B
choices.body: 48-bit flat identifiers for NICs on a single link, not globally routable

choices.label: D
choices.body: Hierarchical globally routed like IP prefixes

easy.hint: Next step: ask the scope: one LAN versus the whole Internet.
easy.explanation: MACs name interfaces locally; switches use them on one LAN while routers use hierarchical IPs across networks.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: NIC aa:bb:cc:11:22:33 sends to gateway MAC. Step 2: Router strips those MACs and reframes toward the next hop. Step 3: Original MACs never leave the first LAN.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: DNS returns IPs, never MACs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: MACs belong to hardware; ports identify connections.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: MACs are flat and link-local; IPs aggregate hierarchically.

easy.prompt: ARP on an Ethernet LAN maps…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A hostname to an IP address

choices.label: C
choices.body: An IP address to the MAC address owning it on that subnet

choices.label: D
choices.body: A TCP port to a process

easy.hint: Next step: ask who-has this IP, then cache the tell reply.
easy.explanation: ARP requests broadcast who-has; the owner unicasts its MAC. ND does this for IPv6.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Host broadcasts ARP who-has 10.0.0.1 tell 10.0.0.5. Step 2: Gateway replies 10.0.0.1 is-at de:ad:01. Step 3: Sender caches and frames IP packets to that MAC.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: DNS maps names to IPs, not ARP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: HTTP fetches resources; ARP resolves link addresses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Ports demultiplex locally; ARP maps LAN addresses.

easy.prompt: Classic Ethernet hubs versus switches differ in that hubs…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Repeat every bit out all ports, sharing one collision domain

easy.hint: Next step: count collision domains: one per hub versus one per switch port.
easy.explanation: Hubs broadcast electrically; switches learn MAC-to-port and filter unicast, giving each port its own domain.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Host A sends frame dst bb:..:02 into a hub. Step 2: Hub repeats it out all ports including C's. Step 3: A switch would send only toward port 2 after learning.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is switching, the opposite of hub flooding.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Neither hubs nor basic switches encrypt.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Hubs are layer-1 repeaters; they never read IP.

easy.prompt: A switch learns MAC addresses by…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Recording the source MAC with the ingress port of each frame

easy.hint: Next step: watch the source field on arrival, the dst field for forwarding.
easy.explanation: Learning builds MAC->port tables so later unicast floods only toward the destination.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Frame src aa:..:01 arrives port 3. Step 2: Table records aa:..:01 -> port 3. Step 3: Later frame dst aa:..:01 exits only port 3.

hard.hint: Next step: compare per-hop IPv4 option parsing with end-to-end chains.
hard.explanation: Only endpoints (or designated hops) parse most extensions; routers fast-path the base header.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Packet carries base header + Fragment + ESP extensions. Step 2: Core routers read base dst and forward, skipping chains. Step 3: Destination parses Fragment offset then decrypts ESP payload.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Avoiding that parsing is the point of extensions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Base header still carries 128-bit addresses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Only sources fragment in IPv6, never transit routers.

hard.prompt: TDMA versus contention access trade off…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Guaranteed slots with idle waste versus statistical sharing with collision risk

hard.hint: Next step: ask what an idle user costs in each scheme.
hard.explanation: TDMA wastes empty slots but bounds delay; contention reuses idle time but collapses under overload.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 4-station TDMA leaves 3 slots idle when only A sends. Step 2: Contention lets A use all airtime at low load. Step 3: At overload, collisions slash contention goodput while TDMA holds steady.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Access control is about medium sharing, not crypto.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Naming caches are unrelated to slot sharing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Physics appearance never sets MAC efficiency.

hard.prompt: Checksums (Internet) versus CRCs (link) differ in that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: CRCs run at the app layer

choices.label: B
choices.body: Ones-complement sums catch header typos cheaply; CRC polynomials catch wire bursts strongly

hard.hint: Next step: place each check where it runs: endpoints versus every hop.
hard.explanation: IP/TCP checksums are software-cheap end-to-end; Ethernet CRC is hardware-strong per hop.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: IP header sum validates version, TTL, addresses at each router. Step 2: Ethernet CRC-32 validates the whole frame including that IP packet. Step 3: A burst flipping 4 bits passes the sum but fails CRC.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: CRCs protect link frames in NIC hardware.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Strength and cost differ by design point.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: CRC math is strictly stronger for bursts.

hard.prompt: Hidden versus exposed terminals differ in that hidden nodes…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Are both fixed by higher transmit power

choices.label: C
choices.body: Cannot hear each other but collide at the receiver; exposed nodes defer needlessly

hard.hint: Next step: draw who hears whom around the AP.
hard.explanation: RTS/CTS or collision-avoidance helps hidden pairs; exposed pairs need spatial reuse/MAC tuning instead.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: A and C both reach AP but not each other. Step 2: Simultaneous DATA garbles at AP (hidden). Step 3: Meanwhile B near A defers to D's flow it would not disturb (exposed).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hidden collisions directly cut airtime goodput.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: More power worsens exposed deferral and interference.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Switches segment wires; radio hearing is the issue.

hard.prompt: STP reconvergence after a link failure is slow classically because…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Ports transition Listen->Learn->Forward with timers to avoid transient loops

hard.hint: Next step: trace port states and BPDU propagation after the break.
hard.explanation: Timer-driven states (plus max-age) trade speed for loop safety; RSTP adds handshake roles to converge fast.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Root port dies; BPDUs stop arriving. Step 2: Max-age expiry triggers re-election of root/designated. Step 3: New port steps Listen (15 s) then Learn (15 s) before Forward.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Propagation is fast; state timers dominate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Transport recovery follows; STP moves first.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Naming TTLs never gate L2 convergence.

hard.prompt: Why can't MAC addresses route globally like IP?

choices.label: C
choices.body: They are too long at 48 bits

choices.label: D
choices.body: They are flat with no aggregation prefix, so tables would need every host

hard.hint: Next step: compare longest-prefix aggregation with flat exact lookup.
hard.explanation: IP hierarchies summarize millions into one entry; flat MACs need per-host entries that explode core tables.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: ISP advertises 203.0.113.0/24 as one BGP entry for 256 hosts. Step 2: Flat MACs would need 256 exact entries for the same hosts. Step 3: At Internet scale billions of exact entries are infeasible.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: MACs are stable NIC IDs; topology mobility is the issue.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DNS scope is naming; aggregation is the routing reason.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 48 bits is shorter than 128-bit IPv6; length is not the blocker.

hard.prompt: Byte stuffing in framing solves…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Payload bytes that look like flags by escaping them transparently

hard.hint: Next step: find flag pattern 0x7E inside data and escape it.
hard.explanation: DLE/escape bytes distinguish real delimiters from data copies, preserving transparency without banning values.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Payload contains 0x7E flag-like byte. Step 2: Sender inserts escape 0x7D 0x5E on the wire. Step 3: Receiver strips escape and restores 0x7E data, keeping one real end flag.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Address space is unrelated to delimiters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Window control is separate from transparency.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Reflection abuse is unrelated to stuffing.

hard.prompt: Exponential backoff after collisions provides…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Stability by spreading retries, at the cost of unfairness and delay jitter

hard.hint: Next step: double the window each collision and pick randomly.
hard.explanation: Random spreading breaks sync, but unlucky stations wait long while winners capture. Bounded-Delay schemes differ.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: A and B collide; both pick 0/1 slots. Step 2: They collide again; window grows 0-3 slots. Step 3: A picks 0 and streams while B backs off repeatedly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Random picks never assign ownership.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Delay grows sharply with contention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Backoff is probabilistic and can starve losers.

hard.prompt: A switch MAC-table overflow attack works by…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Flooding fake sources so legit entries age out and traffic floods

hard.hint: Next step: fill the finite CAM, then watch unicast become broadcast.
hard.explanation: Exhausted tables fail open to flooding, letting the attacker sniff. Port security limits MACs per port.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Attacker sends 8000 frames with random src MACs port 1. Step 2: CAM fills; victim MAC entry evicts. Step 3: Frames to the victim flood all ports including the attacker's tap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: App traffic does not fill L2 CAM tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: TTL affects L3 lifetime, not CAM capacity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Naming caches are separate from MAC tables.

hard.prompt: WPA2-PSK versus open Wi-Fi differ in that PSK…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Authenticates the link and encrypts frames, but all insiders share the key

hard.hint: Next step: separate link encryption among insiders from endpoint trust.
hard.explanation: PSK stops outsiders sniffing airtime, yet any insider can decrypt peers' frames. TLS still needed end-to-end.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Client 4-way handshake derives PTK from PSK. Step 2: DATA frames carry CCMP-encrypted payloads over radio. Step 3: A second insider with the PSK captures and decrypts those frames.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Radio crypto ends at the AP; Internet path needs TLS.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MACs stay link-local regardless of crypto.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Certificates authenticate servers; PSK is shared link secret.

hard.prompt: TLS 1.3 versus 1.2 handshake differs mainly by…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Fewer round trips with ephemeral-only key shares and encrypted extensions

hard.hint: Next step: count RTTs and note what is now encrypted.
hard.explanation: 1.3 guesses key shares in the first flight and encrypts most extensions, cutting setup latency.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: ClientHello carries key_share immediately. Step 2: ServerHello plus EncryptedExtensions return in 1 RTT. Step 3: Finished verifies; app data follows sooner than 1.2's ~2 RTT.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Certs (or PSK) still authenticate the peer.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 1.3 strengthens crypto, never removes it.

hard.prompt: Domain-validated (DV) versus extended-validation (EV) certs differ in that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: DV proves control of the name; EV additionally vets organization identity

choices.label: C
choices.body: DV proves the content is safe

hard.hint: Next step: ask what was vetted: the name, or the legal entity too.
hard.explanation: Both encrypt equally; neither vouches for content honesty. Browsers now treat them similarly in UI.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Attacker passes HTTP-01 challenge for lookalike domain, gets DV. Step 2: Handshake validates to the lookalike cleanly. Step 3: EV would demand company documents — still no content safety proof.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DV is automated challenge-based.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No cert type audits content honesty.

hard.prompt: HTTP range requests (206 Partial Content) help…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Resume downloads and fetch segments in parallel

hard.hint: Next step: ask how a client resumes byte 10M of 100M.
hard.explanation: Range headers request slices; servers reply 206 with Content-Range. Clients stitch or resume.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Client sends GET with Range: bytes=10000000-. Step 2: Server replies 206 Content-Range 10000000-…/total. Step 3: Downloader fetches four ranges concurrently and concatenates.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Naming is DNS, unaffected.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Link addressing is unrelated.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: TLS encrypts; ranges only slice.

hard.prompt: Stale-while-revalidate improves perceived latency by…

choices.label: A

hard.hint: Next step: compare block-on-revalidate with serve-now-update-later.
hard.explanation: Clients get instant (marked stale) bytes; caches converge without stalling renders.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: Entry age 70 s with stale-while-revalidate=30. Step 2: Request gets instant stale body. Step 3: Cache revalidates with If-None-Match and updates for next hits.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Background revalidation still contacts origin.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Blocking is what this directive avoids.

hard.prompt: QUIC 0-RTT early data risks…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Replay of non-idempotent requests by observers or servers

hard.explanation: Replayed early data may re-execute; only idempotent GETs should use 0-RTT, with anti-replay limits.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Addressing is unaffected.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Capacity is unchanged.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Latency still obeys physics.

hard.prompt: TCP sequence-guessing (blind spoofing) is hard today because…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Random ISNs plus large windows and firewalls reject off-window forgeries

hard.explanation: Attackers must hit the in-window seq plus matching four-tuple without seeing traffic. Random ISNs make this infeasible.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Stateful filters drop unsolicited segments.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Seq numbers remain core to TCP.

hard.prompt: NSEC/NSEC3 in DNSSEC exist to…
